questions.prompt: A constriction can increase both the effective mass and stiffness of air. Why do those effects not simply cancel everywhere?
questions.answer: A mode’s regions of strong motion and strong compression are not the same. Increased mass matters most where air moves strongly, while increased stiffness matters most where compression is strong. Their relative contributions depend on the constriction location and the mode being considered.
rubric: The answer distinguishes regions of strong motion from regions of strong compression.
The answer explains that local mode structure determines which perturbation effect dominates.

questions.prompt: What remains the same and what changes when the illustrated 100 Hz harmonic source passes through the schwa filter?
questions.answer: The harmonic frequencies retain their 100 Hz spacing. The filter changes their relative amplitudes, strengthening harmonics near its resonances and weakening others. The resulting spectral envelope carries the vowel pattern rather than creating a different source spacing.
rubric: The answer preserves the harmonic frequency spacing.
The answer attributes relative harmonic-height changes and the spectral envelope to the filter.

questions.prompt: How can /i/ and /a/ have different formant patterns even when the source harmonic spacing is identical?
questions.answer: The source can supply the same set of harmonics while different vocal-tract shapes filter their amplitudes differently. The illustrated /i/ has a low F1 and high F2, while /a/ has a higher F1 and lower F2. Different resonance envelopes can therefore produce different vowels without changing the source spacing.
rubric: The answer explains that different filters act on a shared harmonic source.
The answer correctly compares the illustrated F1/F2 patterns of /i/ and /a/.

questions.prompt: How is the information in one spectrum rearranged when many spectra are assembled into the illustrated spectrogram?
questions.answer: Each spectrum supplies amplitudes at different frequencies for one short time slice. In the spectrogram, frequency runs vertically and the time slices are laid out horizontally. Larger spectral amplitudes become darker marks in this grayscale display.
rubric: The answer maps spectrum frequency to the spectrogram’s vertical axis and successive slices to time.
The answer maps amplitude to darkness in the illustrated grayscale display.

questions.prompt: Why can it become harder to estimate a vowel’s formants when the fundamental frequency is high?
questions.answer: Higher fundamental frequency spaces the source harmonics farther apart. Fewer harmonic samples then describe the resonance envelope, making a broad formant pattern harder to distinguish from individual harmonic peaks. The problem concerns sampling the filter with sparse harmonics, rather than formants automatically disappearing.
rubric: The answer connects higher F0 to wider harmonic spacing.
The answer explains that fewer harmonic samples make the resonance envelope harder to identify.

questions.prompt: One printed list in Lecture 12 says stiffness rises while frequency falls, but its later bullet and Lecture 13 disagree. Which relationship should guide your explanation?
questions.answer: Use increasing stiffness raises frequency when mass and the relevant system conditions are held fixed. Lecture 13 corrects the arrow, and the explanation agrees with the stronger restoring action and with the comparative mass–spring demonstration.
rubric: The answer uses the corrected positive stiffness–frequency relationship under fixed comparison conditions.

questions.prompt: How does mass-and-stiffness reasoning connect hearing with speech production without making them the same process?
questions.answer: In hearing, varying mechanical properties help different basilar-membrane regions respond to different frequencies. In speech production, changing vocal-fold properties changes the source vibration, while vocal-tract constrictions change resonance patterns. Mechanical properties shape frequency responses in each case, but the structures and roles differ.
rubric: The answer connects hearing to region-dependent frequency response.
The answer distinguishes the speech source and vocal-tract resonances while stating their shared mechanical principle.

rubric: Interpret a shared formant as a partial match.
Use the full resonance pattern rather than one label.
questions.topic: Shared higher formant and vowel identity

questions.prompt: Under the illustrated grayscale key, a band stays at the same vertical frequency but becomes darker as time advances. What change is represented?

options.text: The frequency increases while amplitude remains fixed, because darker ink indicates a higher point on the frequency axis.
options.feedback: Frequency would require a vertical-position change. Darkness encodes amplitude here.

options.text: The source pitch decreases, because a darker mark is the display’s way of representing a larger gap between adjacent harmonics.
options.feedback: A band’s darkness does not measure harmonic spacing or source pitch.

options.text: The band’s duration increases, because darker marks represent longer persistence of a sound when the vertical frequency position stays fixed.
options.feedback: The legend maps darkness to amplitude. Duration follows horizontal extent or elapsed time, rather than the shade of a mark.

options.text: Amplitude at that frequency increases while its frequency position remains unchanged in the display.
options.feedback: The source maps amplitude to darkness and frequency to vertical position. A change in one encoding does not require a change in the other.

questions.answer: The source maps amplitude to darkness and frequency to vertical position. A change in one encoding does not require a change in the other.
rubric: Read darkness using the supplied amplitude key.
Keep frequency position distinct from amplitude.

questions.prompt: Suppose the same short-time spectra are placed on a spectrogram in reverse time order without changing any individual spectrum. Which property changes?

options.text: The stronger amplitudes in each slice become weaker, because moving a slice to a different horizontal position reverses the darkness key.
options.feedback: Horizontal ordering and amplitude encoding are different operations.

options.text: The direction of the displayed vowel transition reverses, while each individual time slice retains its frequency–amplitude information.
options.feedback: A spectrogram preserves the order of successive spectra. Reversing that order reverses the trajectory through time but does not alter the contents of a particular spectrum.

options.text: The harmonic frequencies inside each original slice are reversed in sign, because time reversal of the display exchanges frequency and amplitude axes.
options.feedback: Reordering slices does not exchange their axes or change their recorded component values.

options.text: The formant bands remain in the same temporal sequence, because a spectrogram is an average spectrum that discards ordering before it is drawn.
options.feedback: The source explicitly stacks spectra over time, preserving their order.

questions.answer: A spectrogram preserves the order of successive spectra. Reversing that order reverses the trajectory through time but does not alter the contents of a particular spectrum.
rubric: Recognize the time-order information supplied by stacking.
Separate reordering slices from changing their contents.

questions.prompt: You want to test whether wider source spacing obscures formants without changing the filter itself. Which comparison isolates that issue most directly?

options.text: Hold the illustrated resonance envelope fixed, vary the source harmonic spacing, and compare how the available line heights reveal that same envelope.
options.feedback: The source comparison changes F0 while holding the filter fixed. This isolates the density of harmonic samples rather than combining pitch differences with new resonance locations.

options.text: Compare different vowels and different source pitches together, attributing any difference in visible bands to pitch without tracking the changed resonances.
options.feedback: Changing both source and filter confounds the explanation of the visible bands.

options.text: Hold the source spacing fixed but move the resonance peaks, using the resulting envelope difference as evidence that the source samples became sparser.
options.feedback: That manipulates the filter rather than source sampling density.

options.text: Compare the total amplitudes of two recordings without examining their harmonic positions, treating the louder one as the more densely sampled filter.
options.feedback: Overall amplitude does not measure the spacing of the available harmonic samples.

questions.answer: The source comparison changes F0 while holding the filter fixed. This isolates the density of harmonic samples rather than combining pitch differences with new resonance locations.
rubric: Hold filter conditions fixed.
Vary harmonic spacing and inspect how it samples the envelope.

questions.prompt: In a high-F0 spectrum, one strong harmonic appears near a resonance region but few neighbors sample the envelope. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The strong harmonic’s frequency directly establishes the exact formant, because high F0 makes a sample and its underlying resonance the same physical quantity.
options.feedback: Wider spacing reduces evidence about the envelope rather than making a component identical to a resonance.

options.text: The filter has lost the neighboring formants, because the lack of nearby source components means those resonance mechanisms no longer exist in the tract.
options.feedback: A sparse source can leave resonances poorly sampled without removing them from the filter.

options.text: The exact formant location is less securely revealed by that isolated line; its frequency is a sample of the filter response rather than proof of the envelope’s peak.
options.feedback: Sparse harmonics can obscure the resonance envelope. A strong available sample can lie near a formant without locating the resonance exactly or proving that other resonances are absent.

options.text: The strong line establishes a lower F0 than the dense-source example, because fewer neighboring components indicate more closely spaced repetitions.
options.feedback: Fewer harmonics in a fixed frequency region reflect wider spacing and higher F0 in the comparison.

questions.answer: Sparse harmonics can obscure the resonance envelope. A strong available sample can lie near a formant without locating the resonance exactly or proving that other resonances are absent.
rubric: Treat an isolated harmonic as a sample rather than an exact resonance measurement.
Distinguish absent samples from absent resonances.
questions.topic: Limits of an isolated spectral peak

questions.prompt: The mode atlas scales panels to the same largest displayed displacement. What can a learner compare reliably without treating equal drawing height as an unscaled physical-amplitude measurement?

options.text: The modes have equal frequencies because matching their maximum displacements removes the temporal differences between their oscillations.
options.feedback: Amplitude normalization does not equalize their rates.

options.text: The higher-mode colors identify heavier masses, so the matched heights allow frequency differences to be assigned to mass rather than mode shape.
options.feedback: The atlas colors identify mode number, and the compared rows specify their mechanical conditions.

options.text: The modes have equal unscaled physical amplitudes because matching their drawn peak heights makes the panel-specific display scaling irrelevant to the comparison.
options.feedback: The source scales the drawings for visibility. Matched graphic heights do not remove the need to consider those display scales.

options.text: The spatial patterns and relative motion rates can be compared, while the matched displayed heights do not establish equal unscaled amplitudes across modes.
options.feedback: The source states that displayed displacement scales are normalized for visibility. The atlas emphasizes shape and rate, so equal graphic height does not independently establish equal unscaled motion amplitudes.

questions.answer: The source states that displayed displacement scales are normalized for visibility. The atlas emphasizes shape and rate, so equal graphic height does not independently establish equal unscaled motion amplitudes.
rubric: Recognize display normalization as a presentation condition.
Compare mode shape and rate without treating matched graphic heights as an independent physical-amplitude result.

questions.prompt: A student estimates the fixed–free fundamental by taking the common gap between neighboring allowed resonance peaks in the illustrated 100, 300, 500, 700 Hz sequence. Explain why this method confuses two quantities.
questions.answer: The fundamental is the lowest allowed frequency, illustrated as 100 Hz. Neighboring allowed modes are separated by gaps that skip the missing even multiples. Their gap is therefore not the same quantity as the fundamental. Mode spacing in this resonance sequence should not be confused with the consecutive harmonic spacing of a voiced source comb.
rubric: Identify the fundamental as the lowest illustrated allowed frequency.
Explain that the odd-multiple sequence skips intervening multiples.
Distinguish allowed-mode spacing from consecutive source-harmonic spacing.
questions.topic: Fundamental versus gaps between allowed resonances

questions.prompt: You compare two drawings with different numbers of half-wave packets and want to conclude that the drawing with more packets has the higher frequency. What conditions must be shared for the lecture’s explanation to justify that comparison?
questions.answer: The drawings must represent the same physical length, the same boundary type, and the same wave-speed conditions of the ideal string comparison. More packets then mean a shorter wavelength within that length and a faster vibration. If length or wave speed also changes, packet count by itself is insufficient to establish the rate ordering across the two systems.
rubric: Hold length and the relevant wave-speed conditions fixed.
Preserve the boundary assumptions used to define the packet patterns.
Connect more packets within that common length to a shorter wavelength and higher frequency.

questions.prompt: The pickup spectrum has equal heights for five string components. A learner concludes that each mode has equal displacement at every point of the string. What information has the learner overlooked?
questions.answer: The spectrum was measured at one marked position, and the modal amplitudes were chosen to produce equal peaks there. Each mode has its own spatial displacement pattern, including nodes and regions of stronger movement. Matching the measured contributions at one location does not establish equal displacement at other locations or across the whole string.
rubric: Retain the specified measurement location and chosen modal amplitudes.
Explain position-dependent displacement within a mode.
Reject the inference from a local match to an everywhere match.
questions.topic: From local spectral amplitude to a global claim

questions.prompt: A still frame of an oscillating mode happens to show very little displacement from the resting line. What additional observation would you need before deciding that the mode is absent or has stopped?
questions.answer: I would examine how the displacement changes over time or inspect the measured signal over an interval. A single frame gives a phase-dependent position rather than the complete repeating motion. A mode can pass close to its resting line while continuing to oscillate, so small displacement in one image does not establish that its contribution is absent.
rubric: Distinguish an instantaneous position from a time-dependent motion.
Request temporal evidence rather than treating one frame as a complete measurement.

questions.prompt: The air-column display separates Mode1@F1, Mode2@F2, and Mode3@F3 into different rows. Why should those rows not be interpreted as three independent streams of air traveling through different vocal tracts?
questions.answer: The rows isolate different resonance patterns of the same modeled air column. They let us compare where that air moves or compresses in each mode. The physical air system can support contributions from several modes; drawing those contributions separately does not create separate anatomical streams or tracts.
rubric: Identify the rows as isolated modes of one air system.
Explain the purpose of separating patterns for comparison.
Distinguish modal decomposition from separate physical streams.
questions.topic: Several mode panels, one air system

questions.prompt: At a chosen location, a mode has small displacement but strong compression. You want to raise that mode’s frequency while avoiding a large mass-loading effect. What local comparison would most directly test the lecture’s mechanism?
questions.answer: Compare an increase in effective local stiffness at that strongly compressed region while keeping the other relevant conditions fixed. The mode deforms that region strongly, so the stiffness increase should contribute an upward frequency shift. Added mass there has a relatively small effect because the mode’s displacement at that location is small. The test should separate the intended stiffness change from simultaneous uncontrolled changes.
rubric: Identify strong compression as sensitivity to stiffness.
Predict an upward frequency effect under the fixed comparison.
Use small displacement to explain reduced sensitivity to added mass.
questions.topic: Choosing a local perturbation to test

questions.prompt: The /u/ illustration lowers both F1 and F2, whereas /a/ raises F1 but lowers F2. Explain why their shared F2 direction and opposite F1 directions can follow the same mass-and-stiffness principles.
questions.answer: Near the lip loading of /u/, motion dominates for both modes, so added mass lowers both frequencies. Near the illustrated /a/ constriction, compression and stiffness dominate the first mode, raising F1, while motion and mass dominate the second, lowering F2. The common physical rules are weighted differently by location in each mode; the mass rule itself has not reversed.
rubric: Explain the mass-dominated first and second modes of /u/.
Explain stiffness dominance for /a/ F1 and mass dominance for /a/ F2.
Attribute the contrast to location and mode shape rather than a reversed physical rule.
questions.topic: Comparing /u/ and /a/ without reversing the rule

questions.prompt: The diagram places dean and dune in the high-vowel region. Why would treating “high vowel” as a complete prediction of the first two formant shifts miss an important difference in the supplied models?
questions.answer: Height is one articulatory dimension, while the constrictions also differ in front–back location and lip involvement. The /i/-like dean comparison places a constriction near two-thirds from the glottis, giving lower F1 and higher F2. The /u/-like dune comparison loads the lip end, giving lower F1 and lower F2. Their shared height does not make their local effects on the second mode identical.
rubric: Distinguish tongue height from the complete constriction location.
Compare the different F2 effects in the supplied /i/ and /u/ models.
Connect those effects to mode-specific local motion or deformation.
questions.topic: Articulatory height does not specify the whole perturbation

questions.prompt: In the “same vowel, three pitches” comparison, identify what is varied, what is held fixed, and which conclusion about an apparent change in the visible bands is supported.
questions.answer: The source spacing is varied across the illustrated pitch conditions while the filter remains fixed at the stated resonance locations. Wider spacing gives fewer harmonic samples of that filter, so the visible bands or peaks can look less like a continuous formant envelope. This comparison supports a sampling explanation for the display change, rather than establishing that the tract’s resonances moved between conditions.
rubric: Identify source harmonic spacing as the manipulated variable.
Identify the filter resonance pattern as controlled.
Interpret display changes as different sampling under those conditions.
questions.topic: Identifying the controlled comparison in the high-pitch figure

questions.prompt: The schwa figure contains closely spaced source lines and much more widely separated labeled formant regions. Explain why estimating F0 from the separation of F1 and F2 would use the wrong series.
questions.answer: F0 determines the spacing of the consecutive source harmonics, shown 100 Hz apart. F1 and F2 label different resonances of the vocal-tract filter, not adjacent source components. Their separation describes part of the filter pattern rather than the vocal folds’ repetition rate. The two frequency organizations coexist in the same filtered spectrum.
rubric: Use consecutive source harmonics to identify the relevant F0 spacing.
Distinguish formant labels as filter resonances rather than source harmonics.
questions.topic: Two different frequency spacings in the schwa figure

questions.prompt: You want to describe how amplitude at one chosen frequency changes during the vowel transition. How would you read that information from the illustrated spectrogram and relate it to the sequence of spectra?
questions.answer: I would keep the same vertical frequency position and follow its darkness from left to right through time using the amplitude key. Each time slice corresponds to the height at that frequency in its spectrum. This traces amplitude changes at a fixed frequency, rather than following a moving formant band and therefore changing which frequency is being sampled.
rubric: Hold the frequency coordinate fixed and move along time.
Decode darkness as amplitude using the supplied key.
Relate each time slice to a spectral height at the same frequency.

questions.prompt: Imagine a copy of the spectrogram has been printed with its light–dark scale reversed, and the key clearly labels light as high amplitude. What should change in your reading, and what should remain the same?
questions.answer: Amplitude must be interpreted using the new key rather than the original black-is-high convention. Frequency still follows vertical position, and time still follows horizontal position if those axes have not changed. Reversing the visual encoding does not by itself move a resonance, change the source pitch, or reverse the temporal order.
rubric: Apply the stated amplitude key instead of assuming darkness has a fixed meaning.
Keep unchanged frequency and time axes separate from the changed shading convention.

questions.prompt: During a hypothetical interval, the first band rises while retaining the same darkness, and the second stays at the same frequency but becomes darker. Describe these two changes without treating frequency and amplitude as interchangeable.
questions.answer: The first band moves to a higher frequency with no indicated change in its encoded amplitude under the stated conditions. The second band gains amplitude at an unchanged frequency. Vertical movement and darkness carry different information, so one change cannot be inferred from the other.
rubric: Read the first band’s vertical movement as a frequency change.
Read the second band’s darkening as an amplitude change.
Keep each unchanged quantity explicit.
questions.topic: Separating two changes in one spectrogram

questions.prompt: The lecture uses toddler and soprano pitch examples to motivate the sampling problem. Why would it overstate the source to report that the schematic has measured the formants of all toddlers or all sopranos?
questions.answer: The examples illustrate how wider harmonic spacing can make a filter harder to sample, and the graphic holds a schematic filter fixed for that comparison. It is not a supplied participant dataset establishing universal anatomy, formant values, or outcomes for either group. The supported claim concerns the source-spacing mechanism, not measured values for an entire population.
rubric: Identify the demonstration’s mechanism and fixed-filter conditions.
Distinguish schematic examples from participant measurements.
Avoid turning illustrative pitch values into universal formant values.
questions.topic: Schematic comparison versus a population claim

questions.prompt: Consider two hypothetical comparisons. In A, the harmonic spacing is retained but the relative-height envelope is reshaped. In B, the envelope is retained while the harmonic spacing widens. Explain which part of the source–filter account is manipulated in each and what you would inspect to check it.
questions.answer: In A, the filter emphasis changes while the source spacing is retained; I would compare resonance-envelope locations and relative harmonic heights. In B, the source repetition rate changes while the filter is held fixed; I would compare the distances between source components and how densely they sample the retained envelope. A change in pitch and a change in vowel filtering therefore require different evidence, even though both affect the observed spectrum.
rubric: Assign A to changed filtering under retained source spacing.
Assign B to changed source spacing under retained filtering.
Name the spectral evidence appropriate to each manipulation.
